Portfolio · Electrical BIM Engineer

From single‑line diagram to issued drawing, automated in Revit.

I work on the electrical side of large building projects: substations, LV switchboards, distribution boards, containment and the drawing packages that describe them. A lot of that work is the same task done hundreds of times: balancing a board, tagging a tray, copying a load onto a single-line diagram, checking a shop drawing against the spec.

So I started writing my own tools. Fifty of them now run on our Revit ribbon, written in Python on pyRevit, each one built around a real task from a live project and refined from what went wrong when it first ran on a real model.

Why I built them

The repetitive half of an electrical drawing package

On an electrical BIM job the model is only the start. Every board needs a schedule that is balanced across three phases. Every load has to reach the single-line diagram. Every tray run needs a size, a tag on the plan and a check against the cable calculation. Every contractor submittal has to be read against the specification.

None of it is difficult, but all of it is slow, and mistakes creep in through copying. My tools take the copying out. They read what is already in the model, the Excel calculations or the PDFs, show the result for checking, and write it back in one step that a single Undo can reverse.

Model→Boards & circuits→Single-line diagram→ Containment→Drawings→Review & QA
Case studies

Seven pieces of work, start to finish

Balanced panel schedules in one pass

Panel Schedule Manager takes a board from "circuits connected" to "schedule issued": phase balancing, spares and spaces, way arrangement and the schedule view itself.

The problem

Balancing a 36-way board by hand means moving circuits between ways and re-adding loads per phase, then doing it again when a load changes. Spares were added afterwards and often all landed on one or two phases.

What it does

  • Balances single- and three-pole circuits across R, Y and B to a target imbalance
  • Adds spares and spaces to each board type's standard (PP, LP, ELP, UDB, ACP)
  • Spreads spares over the free ways of every phase, not just the next empty way
  • Moves circuits between ways through free "staging" ways, so a full board never locks up

How it works

A five-step window: choose panels, set rules, set spares, preview every move, execute. The whole run is one transaction group, so one Undo restores the board.

Cable trays: sized, drawn and tagged

Three tools cover the containment drawings: Tray Layout draws the cross-section of every tray from the cable schedule, Tag Tray Runs annotates the plans, and Cable Tray QA/QC checks one against the other.

The problem

A basement plan can hold a hundred and fifty tray runs. Each needs its tag beside the right tray, clear of the others, and the tag has to agree with the cable calculation in Excel. Done by hand, tags overlap and sizes drift from the calculation.

What it does

  • Tray Layout reads the cable schedule and draws one section per tray, with cable spacing and 20 % future space
  • Tag Tray Runs puts one tag per run, repeated every 15 m, and keeps leaders from crossing or lying on each other
  • Cable Tray QA/QC compares sheet tags with the calculation list and exports a coloured Excel report

How it works

The tagging works on a spatial index of every tray, tag, text note and grid in the view, and tries candidate positions in rings around each run until it finds a clear one.

Shop drawing review against the specification

Shop Drawing Review reads the contractor's PDF and the specification PDFs, finds where they disagree, and writes a marked-up copy with revision clouds, numbered bubbles and a comment sheet.

The problem

Reviewing an LV switchboard submittal means checking dozens of values (IP rating, form of separation, short-circuit rating, RAL colour, approved makes, cited standards) against a specification that may run to hundreds of pages.

What it does

  • Finds the relevant specification sections and compares their values with the drawing
  • Flags withdrawn standards, for example IEC 60439 replaced by IEC 61439
  • Adds authority items for SEC, KAHRAMAA, DEWA and ADDC, and an equipment checklist
  • Checks drafting: title block, note numbering, minimum text height, spelling

How it works

It runs entirely on the workstation, with its own PDF reader and writer. The reviewer edits the comment list before anything is written; the original PDF is never changed.

Enlarged electrical rooms, tagged neatly

Enlarged Electrical Rooms creates a cropped plan for every LV, MV, transformer and UPS room found in the architectural model. Auto Tag Layout then tags the equipment the way a drafter would.

The problem

A large project has dozens of electrical rooms, each needing its own enlarged plan and tidy tags. Revit's own tagging puts tags on top of the equipment, so every room was cleaned up by hand.

What it does

  • Finds rooms in the architectural link by name; nearby MV, transformer and LV rooms can be merged into one substation view
  • Places tags in aligned stacks beside the room, with level leaders that do not cross
  • Uses the free paper outside the crop, and stays clear of grid lines and bubbles

How it works

Tags are sorted by the height of the element they point to, so leaders stay level, and each stack is aligned to a common edge. One Undo removes them all.

Loads onto the single-line diagram

Load Transfer copies loads from panels and equipment in the model onto the detail items of the single-line diagram, so the diagram stays in step with the design.

The problem

The single-line diagram is a drafting view, not connected to the model. Every load change meant finding the right symbol and typing the new figure in again.

What it does

  • Pairs each diagram symbol with its model element by a shared value, such as the panel name
  • Refuses to guess: when two elements share a value, the row is marked ambiguous and skipped
  • Shows a full table of old and new values before writing, exportable to CSV
  • Converts units on the way, for example W to kW

How it works

The window stays open while you work in Revit. Model changes go through Revit's external event, and the transfer writes exactly what the review table showed.

Earthing routes around the structure

Create Earthing Routes draws the earthing layout of a plant room: orthogonal lines from each panel to the main earth terminal, around columns, walls and services.

The problem

Earthing drawings are tedious to draw and easy to get wrong. The lines cut through columns or overlap, because nobody re-draws them after the architecture moves.

What it does

  • Finds a clear orthogonal path for each panel, keeping a set clearance from obstacles
  • Reads obstacles from the host model and from the architectural and structural links
  • Shows a preview, then draws detail lines only, with no 3D geometry added

Excel schedules as native Revit tables

Table Gen reads an Excel sheet directly from its file and draws it in Revit with its Excel look, then keeps it in step: when the Excel changes, one click redraws the table where it sits on the sheet.

The problem

Cable schedules, load summaries and equipment lists live in Excel. Pasting them into Revit as images goes out of date; retyping them takes hours.

What it does

  • Keeps number formats, merged cells, bold text, alignment, wrapping, borders and fills
  • Uses the project's own text types and line styles, so office standards stay intact
  • Widens columns where Revit's font runs wider than Excel's

How it works

It creates every text first, measures them all in one pass, then places them. The first version measured each text after moving the previous one, which made Revit redraw the view hundreds of times.

Working rules

How I build them

Show it before writing it

Tools that change model data first show the change: old and new values, matched pairs, proposed ratings.

One Undo

A run is one transaction or transaction group, so a single Undo returns the model to where it was.

Never touch the links

Architectural and structural links are read for rooms, grids and clashes, and never edited.

Don't guess

Two possible sources for one target, or a type parameter where an instance one is needed: flagged and skipped.

Read files directly

Excel and PDF are read from their file formats. No Excel installation, no cloud service.

Fix from the log

The larger tools log each run, so a problem on a live model is fixed from evidence rather than guesswork.
